Inbound FastJson @type payload with jar:/ldap:/rmi: reference to Spring Boot app (CVE-2026-16723) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP request bodies/URIs carrying a FastJson '@type' key alongside a nested jar:, ldap:, rmi: URL or JdbcRowSetImpl/dataSourceName reference — the exploitation shape for CVE-2026-16723 against internet-facing Spring Boot fat-JAR apps. Article-specific because it keys on the @type + remote-resource-lookup combination, not generic deserialization. Rationale: Keys on the CVE-2026-16723 exploitation signature — a FastJson '@type' key co-occurring with a jar:/ldap:/rmi: remote-resource URL or the JdbcRowSetImpl/dataSourceName lookup class — confirmed by Imperva's advisory and the public jsontype RCE lab. Only expressible on WAF/proxy telemetry that captures request bodies; endpoint EDR/FDR do not ship HTTP bodies, hence Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.imperva.com/blog/imperva-customers-protected-against-cve-2026-16723-critical-fastjson-1-x-zero-day-rce/ • https://github.com/alibaba/fastjson2/wiki/Security-Advisory:-Remote-Code-Execution-in-fastjson-1.2.68%E2%80%931.2.83 • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, Nessus, Nuclei) probing for fastjson with @type test payloads
  • Legitimate APIs that accept a client-supplied field literally named 'type' where the value contains a jar: or ldap: URI
  • Internal red-team / BAS (Picus, SafeBreach) exercises replaying deserialization payloads
  • Log-shipping of stored @type strings in JSON documents that are echoed back into request URLs
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has_any ("nuclei","nessus") or Message has_any ("nuclei","nessus") or SourceIP in ("10.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request from the WAF/proxy for the matched SourceIP; confirm the body contains @type plus a remote jar:/ldap:/rmi: URL and identify the DestinationHostName Spring Boot app and its FastJson version (1.2.68-1.2.83?). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, enable FastJson SafeMode (-Dfastjson.parser.safeMode=true) on the target app, and isolate the app host if outbound class-load already occurred. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'Java outbound LDAP/RMI' and 'Java fat-JAR spawning shell' on the destination host within a 5-minute window of the request to confirm code execution.

Spring Boot Java fat-JAR spawning shell/recon child process (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects a Java process launched as a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar xxx.jar) spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash or a recon binary — the post-exploitation payload of CVE-2026-16723 landing on the app server. Article-specific: it requires the '-jar' parent context Alibaba names as the sole deployment prerequisite. Rationale: Anchors on Alibaba's stated prerequisite — a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar xxx.jar) — as the parent, paired with a shell/recon child, which is the concrete RCE outcome of CVE-2026-16723. Parent+child pairing keeps FP low versus a bare java or bare powershell query. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fastjson-1x-rce-vulnerability-targeted.html • https://github.com/alibaba/fastjson2/wiki/Security-Advisory:-Remote-Code-Execution-in-fastjson-1.2.68%E2%80%931.2.83 • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab
ATT&CKT1190 T1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Jenkins/GitLab/TeamCity build agents (Java) legitimately invoking sh/bash/cmd for build steps
  • Java-based application servers shelling out to certutil/curl for cert or health-check tasks
  • Elastic/Logstash Java agents spawning helper processes
  • Admins running gradlew/mvnw wrappers that fork shells from a java parent
  • Monitoring tooling (Java) calling nslookup/ping for connectivity checks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jenkins","gitlab-runner","teamcity","elastic-agent","logstash") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gradlew","mvnw"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitiatingProcessCommandLine to confirm the fat-jar name and whether the child cmdline shows recon/download (whoami, curl to external IP); correlate with any inbound @type WAF hit on the same host within minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the app server, kill the java parent, and apply FastJson SafeMode or migrate to fastjson2 (no vendor patch exists). 3) Hunt: on the same host review DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound LDAP/RMI (UC below) and any dropped .class/.jar in temp, and sweep the fleet for the same fat-jar name running vulnerable FastJson 1.2.68-1.2.83.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami.exe","whoami","net.exe","curl.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nslookup.exe","ping.exe","id","uname")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","/java")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","/sh","/bash","/dash","whoami","net.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nslookup.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects a Java process launched as a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar) spawning a shell or reconnaissance binary, consistent with RCE via FastJson CVE-2026-16723.

detection:
  selection_parent:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\java.exe OR *\\javaw.exe OR *\\Java.exe) @ParentCommandLine:*-jar* @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\whoami.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\nslookup.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe)

Java application making outbound LDAP/RMI connection (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 remote class load) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects a java -jar process initiating an outbound connection to LDAP (389/636), RMI registry (1099) or the JNDI-exploit-kit LDAP port (1389) on a public host — the attacker-controlled resource lookup FastJson performs before AutoType checks, pulling a malicious class. Article-specific: ties the egress to a Spring Boot fat-JAR process on JNDI/RMI ports. Rationale: Corroborated detection indicator from Imperva/the PoC lab: outbound LDAP/RMI from an app server to an unexpected external host is the JNDI/defineClass remote class-load step. Scoping to a java -jar process on JNDI/RMI ports keeps this high-fidelity; a directory-bound corporate LDAP server is normally internal, not public. Cross-checked against: • https://www.imperva.com/blog/imperva-customers-protected-against-cve-2026-16723-critical-fastjson-1-x-zero-day-rce/ • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab • https://medium.com/@pa2sw0rd/deep-dive-into-fastjson-deserialization-vulnerabilities-from-principles-to-practical-defense-c3be134ec8a6
ATT&CKT1105 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Java app authenticating users against an external/cloud-hosted LDAP directory (e.g. some managed AD/LDAP)
  • Java RMI microservices calling a partner RMI registry over 1099
  • Legacy apps configured with a public LDAP endpoint for address-book lookups
  • Vulnerability scanners generating JNDI callbacks during authorized testing
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP != "" and not (RemoteIP startswith "10." or RemoteIP startswith "192.168." or RemoteIP matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP — is it a known corporate/cloud LDAP or an unfamiliar external host/VPS? Check the fat-jar name and whether a shell child spawned on the same host within seconds. 2) Contain: block egress to the RemoteIP on JNDI/RMI ports from server subnets, isolate the host, and enable FastJson SafeMode on the app. 3) Hunt: capture any class file the JVM fetched, pivot to process-tree UC for java-spawned shells, and enumerate other hosts running FastJson 1.2.68-1.2.83 fat-jars that egressed to the same IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (389, 636, 1099, 1389)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActionType has "Connection"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where RemotePort in (389, 636, 1099, 1389)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Unexpected outbound egress from VeloCloud Orchestrator host (C2 / data exfil)
Inbound connection from known CVE-2026-16812 exploitation IPs to VCO web interface AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound TCP/HTTP(S) connections to the VeloCloud Orchestrator management interface originating from the three IP addresses Arista attributed to active exploitation of the unauthenticated command-injection zero-day. Any hit is a direct IOC match against confirmed attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the three exploitation IPs published in the Arista advisory (verbatim in SA-0144 and CISA KEV) — a direct infrastructure IOC match with no behavioural inference required. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanner or CTI provider that happens to reuse one of these IPs for benign scanning (rare, verify with reverse DNS)
  • Shared-hosting IP later reassigned to a legitimate service after Arista's observation window
  • Internal red-team sourcing from an IP that collides with the IOC set
  • Threat-intel platform test/heartbeat traffic replaying IOC lists
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is a VCO management host and pull the corresponding web access log lines for the source IP — look for encoded chars / internal-service path components around the connection time. 2) Contain: block the three IPs at the perimeter, restrict the VCO web interface to admin networks only, and snapshot logs + filesystem timestamps before any remediation. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same VCO host for web-service→shell process spawns (UC2) and unexpected outbound egress (UC3); if confirmed, treat the appliance as compromised — patch is insufficient, rotate all credentials/certs/keys and validate managed Edge devices.

VeloCloud Orchestrator web service spawning shell for DB export / archive / egress (CVE-2026-16812) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation signature of the VCO OS command-injection flaw: the orchestrator's web tier (nginx/Node.js/Java) spawning a Unix shell or data-handling tool that runs a database dump, archive creation, or outbound fetch. Directly targets Arista's 'unexpected command execution, file creation, database exports, or archive files' IOC guidance. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CWE-78 exploitation outcome Arista called out (unexpected command execution, database export, archive files) by requiring a web-tier parent process spawning a shell/dump/archive/egress tool — a combination that essentially never occurs on a healthy orchestrator appliance. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled DB backup job legitimately invoking mysqldump/pg_dump under a web-service account (verify cron/systemd-timer parentage, not a web-request-driven spawn)
  • Appliance health/telemetry scripts calling curl/wget to Arista update endpoints
  • Vendor support engineer running diagnostic tar/gzip during a maintenance session
  • In-product config-export feature shelling out to tar (validate against expected admin action)
  • Node.js app legitimately spawning sh for a documented internal maintenance task
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("cron","crond","systemd","systemd-cron") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "/etc/cron"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and command line — confirm the parent is the web-facing service and whether the shell ran a DB dump, archive, or egress; correlate the timestamp with inbound web requests (UC1) and access-log anomalies. 2) Contain: isolate the VCO host from the network, kill the offending process, and preserve logs + filesystem timestamps before remediation. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written/archived and any outbound transfers (UC3); if a dump/archive left the host, assume compromise of managed device inventories, credentials, certs and keys — rotate everything and validate/replace the appliance rather than relying on the patch alone.

    or FileName in~ ("mysqldump","pg_dump","pg_dumpall","curl","wget","nc","ncat")

Unexpected outbound egress from VeloCloud Orchestrator host (C2 / data exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound HTTP(S)/TCP initiated by the VCO host — either back to the three known exploitation IPs, or by a web-service/shell process reaching a public address. An orchestrator normally receives management connections, so service-account egress to the internet indicates reverse-shell C2 or exfil of the exported database/archive. Rationale: Combines Arista's 'unexpected outbound HTTP/HTTPS from the VCO host' guidance with the three attributed IPs and a service/shell-process egress filter, so the detection fires on reverse-shell C2 or exfil of the dumped DB even when the destination differs from the published IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VCO reaching Arista/VMware update, licensing, or telemetry endpoints over HTTPS (baseline and allowlist the legitimate FQDNs)
  • NTP/DNS or monitoring-agent egress from the appliance to approved public resolvers
  • Node.js app calling an approved external API (e.g. cloud object storage for legitimate backups)
  • Package-manager (apt/yum) update traffic during a maintenance window
  • Proxy/NAT collapsing many hosts onto the VCO source IP inflating the egress picture
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "arista.com" and RemoteUrl !has "velocloud.net" and RemoteUrl !has "vmware.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the egress destination and the initiating process/command line — is it a known Arista endpoint or an unfamiliar public IP; check bytes-out for bulk transfer consistent with a DB/archive exfil. 2) Contain: block the destination and the three IOC IPs, cut the appliance's outbound internet path, and capture a memory/disk snapshot before remediation. 3) Hunt: tie the egress back to a web-service→shell spawn (UC2) and inbound exploit-IP hits (UC1) to confirm the full chain; if exfil is confirmed, rotate all VCO-managed credentials, certificates and cryptographic keys and validate every managed Edge device for tampering.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] IoT/edge SSH & Telnet weak-password brute force followed by successful login · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Dysphoria botnet blockchain C2 resolution via ENS/SNS gateways (.eth/.sol) · [LLM] Dysphoria distribution-node / victim-relay traffic to hardcoded C2 IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Dysphoria botnet blockchain C2 resolution via ENS/SNS gateways (.eth/.sol) AICommand & Control High
Hunts internal hosts resolving the botnet's blockchain name-service records (m3rnbvs5d.eth, burrberry.eth, 24carnforth2merseyside.sol) or reaching public ENS/SNS resolver gateways used to recover the hidden distribution-node list. Enterprise servers and IoT/edge devices almost never touch ENS/Solana name resolution, so this is the headline 'blockchain C2' pivot the campaign introduced. Rationale: Uses the exact ENS/SNS records (m3rnbvs5d.eth, burrberry.eth, 24carnforth2merseyside.sol) plus the public ENS/Solana gateway domains that malware must hit to resolve blockchain names into IPs; corroborated by Nokia Deepfield/Comcast (m3rnbvs5d.eth) and BleepingComputer's ENS/SNS + fake-IPv6 byte-transform write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/ • https://www.nokia.com/blog/breaking-a-botnet-ddos-enigma-code/ • https://corporate.comcast.com/stories/reverse-engineering-jackskid-from-bare-bones-mirai-fork-to-persistent-tv-box-botnet

  • Security researchers detonating malware in a sandbox on the corporate DNS resolver
  • NFT/DeFi marketing team hosts querying Solana mainnet RPC
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling that pre-resolves IOC domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox","firefox.exe","brave","safari")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host from DeviceName/ClientIP; if it is an IoT device, router, camera, or Linux server with no business reason to touch ENS/SNS, treat as compromised. Pull the initiating process/command line. 2) Contain: block the ENS/SNS gateway domains and the resolved distribution-node IPs at egress, isolate the host, and disable remote management/UPnP on the segment. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host's outbound connections to the five distribution-node IPs (UC2), sweep the subnet for other devices resolving the same .eth/.sol records, and check for inbound SSH/Telnet brute force (UC3) preceding the beacon.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteUrl has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol","eth.link","eth.limo","cloudflare-eth.com","api.ensideas.com","mainnet-beta.solana.com")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Name has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol","eth.link","eth.limo","cloudflare-eth.com","api.ensideas.com","mainnet-beta.solana.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResolvedIPs = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Dysphoria distribution-node / victim-relay traffic to hardcoded C2 IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects internal hosts connecting to the five Dysphoria distribution-node IPs (194.87.198.208/104, 194.58.38.79/49/96) where the DDoS sample pulls its HTTP server list and where victim relays forward traffic. Because these IPs are fixed campaign infrastructure, any egress to them from an IoT/edge/server host is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the five extracted distribution-node IPs verbatim; the article states these endpoints are infected machines relaying traffic and that the DDoS sample pulls its server list from them over HTTP, matching the ~5-IP ENS footprint independently reported by Nokia/Comcast. Cross-checked against: • https://www.nokia.com/blog/breaking-a-botnet-ddos-enigma-code/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/EDR tooling actively sinkholing or probing the listed IOC IPs
  • A researcher's detonation VM beaconing from an isolated but logged subnet
  • Shared-hosting reuse if one of the IPs is later reallocated to a benign service (re-validate IOC freshness quarterly)
  • Corporate proxy egress aggregating many hosts behind one SourceIP, obscuring the true origin
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connection direction and the initiating process; inbound to one of these IPs from your relay host vs. outbound from a bot both indicate compromise. 2) Contain: block all five IPs (both directions) at the perimeter, isolate the host, and capture memory/pcap before reimage. 3) Hunt: check the same host for ENS/SNS resolution (UC1) and preceding SSH/Telnet brute force (UC3); enumerate any other internal hosts that touched these IPs and inspect for UPnP port-map / listening relay sockets.

| where RemoteIP in ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DestinationIP in ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96")
   or SourceIP in ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IoT/edge SSH & Telnet weak-password brute force followed by successful login AIExploitation Medium
Detects the botnet's primary entry vector: high-volume SSH/Telnet password guessing from a single external source that culminates in a successful authentication on an internet-facing device. Scoped to failed-then-success correlation per source IP so it surfaces the credential-stuffing foothold Dysphoria uses to re-infect gear after the JackSkid takedown. Rationale: The article and CNCERT/XLab both state weak Telnet and SSH credential guessing is the most consistent entry vector for Dysphoria's post-disruption re-infection; the failed-then-success per-source-IP correlation targets that foothold rather than generic auth noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/ • https://corporate.comcast.com/stories/evolution-of-jackskid-botnet-what-we-found-and-how-residential-proxies-amplify-its-reach
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1078 T1190
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) performing authenticated SSH scans against IoT ranges
  • CI/CD or config-management (Ansible) hosts opening many short-lived SSH sessions
  • A locked-out admin fat-fingering a password repeatedly before succeeding
  • Load-balancer / health-check probes hitting port 22 that generate auth failures
  • Legitimate bastion/jump host with high SSH throughput to managed devices
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP)) and AccountsTried > 1   // real brute force sprays multiple usernames; single-account lockouts are usually benign
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and the target is an internet-facing IoT/edge device; review the account that succeeded and whether it is a default/weak credential. 2) Contain: block the source IP, force-rotate the compromised credential, disable Telnet and password SSH auth on the device, and pull it from public exposure. 3) Hunt: on the compromised device look for immediate outbound to the distribution-node IPs (UC2) or ENS/SNS resolution (UC1), new listening sockets / UPnP port maps, and sweep the subnet for the same source IP hitting other devices.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("LogonFailed","LogonSuccess")
| summarize Failed = countif(ActionType == "LogonFailed"),
            Success = countif(ActionType == "LogonSuccess"),
            AccountsTried = dcount(AccountName),
            FirstFail = minif(Timestamp, ActionType == "LogonFailed"),
            SuccessTime = maxif(Timestamp, ActionType == "LogonSuccess")
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| where Failed >= 20 and Success >= 1   // 20 = brute-force floor for a single source IP
| where SuccessTime > FirstFail
| order by Failed desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName in ("sshd","telnetd","in.telnetd")
| extend SrcIP = extract(@"from (\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend Outcome = case(SyslogMessage has "Failed password" or SyslogMessage has "authentication failure" or SyslogMessage has "Invalid user", "Failed",
                        SyslogMessage has "Accepted password" or SyslogMessage has "Accepted publickey", "Success", "Other")
| where isnotempty(SrcIP) and Outcome != "Other"
| summarize Failed = countif(Outcome == "Failed"), Success = countif(Outcome == "Success"),
            FirstFail = minif(TimeGenerated, Outcome == "Failed"), SuccessTime = maxif(TimeGenerated, Outcome == "Success")
    by Computer, SrcIP
| where Failed >= 20 and Success >= 1   // 20 = brute-force floor per source IP
| where SuccessTime > FirstFail
| order by Failed desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:(sshd OR telnetd OR in.telnetd) ("Failed password" OR "authentication failure" OR "Invalid user")
#event_simpleName=UserLogon
| LogonType=/^(2|3|10)$/
| RemoteAddressIP4=/\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, UserName], function=count())
| _count > 20
# log group: /aws/guardduty/findings
fields @timestamp, type, severity, resource.instanceDetails.instanceId, service.action.networkConnectionAction.remoteIpDetails.ipAddressV4
| filter type like /SSHBruteForce/ or type like /RDPBruteForce/
| sort @timestamp desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count(eval(Authentication.action="failure")) as failures count(eval(Authentication.action="success")) as successes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("sshd","ssh","telnetd","telnet") by Authentication.src Authentication.dest span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where failures >= 20 AND successes >= 1 | sort - failures
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Machine account creation by low-privileged user (Certighost precursor, MachineAccountQuota abuse) · [LLM] AD CS Certification Authority (certsrv.exe) initiating SMB/LDAP to a non-DC host (Certighost chase redirection) · [LLM] AD CS certificate request carrying cdc/rmd chase attributes or targeting a DC account (Certighost enrollment) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New Certighost PoC exploit lets attackers hijack Windows domains
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PKINIT TGT request for a Domain Controller computer account (Certighost forged-cert auth)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DCSync (directory replication) requested by a non-DC principal — krbtgt secret theft
Machine account creation by low-privileged user (Certighost precursor, MachineAccountQuota abuse) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the first stepping-stone of the Certighost (CVE-2026-54121) chain: a non-privileged domain user creating one or more computer accounts under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to obtain a valid principal that satisfies the CA's chase authentication checks. Surfaces creator, new computer account name and volume so an analyst can spot quota abuse preceding a rogue-CA cert request. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit statement that 'a low-privileged user first creates a machine account, which is permitted under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota'. Event 4741 with a non-machine creator is the earliest observable of the chain. Defender XDR does not cleanly emit 4741 as a queryable ActionType, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; the reliable telemetry is DC Security 4741 (Sentinel SecurityEvent / Splunk Change DM). Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/certighost-exploit-lets-low-privileged.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/27/certighost-cve-2026-54121-poc-exploit-released/
ATT&CKT1136.002 T1078.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SCCM/MECM or Autopilot device provisioning workflows joining new endpoints
  • Helpdesk staff staging computer accounts before OS deployment
  • Automation/service accounts that legitimately pre-create machine accounts but are not named with a trailing $
  • VDI/non-persistent desktop pools cycling machine objects
  • Domain-join scripts run under a delegated (but non-admin) user context
Suppression filter
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("svc-sccm","svc-mdt","svc-autopilot") and Computer !in~ ("SCCM01","MDT01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the creator principal and whether it belongs to a provisioning/helpdesk group; check if the new computer account was subsequently used in a certificate enrollment (correlate with UC5) or PKINIT logon (UC3). 2) Contain: if creator is unexpected, disable the newly created machine account(s) and the creator, and set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 to stop further abuse. 3) Hunt: pivot on the creator's workstation for certsrv chase connections (UC2), 4886/4887 requests carrying cdc/rmd (UC5), and any 4662 replication access (UC4) in the following hours.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4741   // A computer account was created
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"   // exclude machine/SYSTEM creators
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("ANONYMOUS LOGON")
| summarize AccountsCreated = dcount(TargetUserName), NewComputers = make_set(TargetUserName, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where AccountsCreated >= 1   // any low-priv creator is worth review; raise for noisy provisioning tools
| order by LastSeen desc

AD CS Certification Authority (certsrv.exe) initiating SMB/LDAP to a non-DC host (Certighost chase redirection) AIExploitation High
Hunts the core Certighost primitive: the CA process being redirected by an attacker-controlled cdc value to connect to a rogue SMB/LSA/LDAP endpoint. A Certification Authority making outbound 445/389/636 connections to a member workstation or attacker host is extremely rare and directly evidences the abused 'chase' fallback. Rationale: Article: 'the CA connects to the server specified in the cdc value and searches for the specified rmd ... systems previously did not verify that the server supplied through the attacker-controlled cdc value was a legitimate domain controller.' A CA (certsrv.exe) opening SMB/LDAP to a non-DC is the direct network artifact of the redirected chase. Sentinel omitted because process-attributed outbound connections (certsrv.exe on 445/389) are not cleanly available in ASIM ImNetworkSession, which lacks the initiating-process field; use Defender/Sysmon on the CA host. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/27/certighost-cve-2026-54121-poc-exploit-released/
ATT&CKT1187 T1649
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CA server legitimately querying its own domain controllers over LDAP/LDAPS during normal enrollment (whitelist DC IPs)
  • Backup/agent software running under certsrv context reaching file shares
  • CA cluster/HA replication traffic to a peer CA
  • Vulnerability scanners probing the CA host that generate reciprocal sessions
  • Certificate template or CRL publishing to an SMB share on a member server
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("10.10.10.10","10.10.10.11")   // replace with your actual DC IPs to suppress legitimate CA->DC LDAP
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the RemoteIP is NOT a domain controller (compare against your DC inventory); pull the concurrent 4886/4887 request on the CA and the cdc/rmd attributes (UC5). 2) Contain: block the rogue RemoteIP, isolate the source machine account host, and if confirmed apply the EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC disable workaround or the July patch on the CA. 3) Hunt: check whether a certificate was issued to a DC computer account and whether PKINIT (UC3) then DCSync (UC4) followed; treat the domain as potentially compromised (krbtgt).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "certsrv.exe"   // the AD CS CA service process
| where RemotePort in (445, 389, 636)   // SMB / LDAP / LDAPS the CA reaches for during a chase
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| summarize ConnCount = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc

DeviceNetworkEvents

| summarize ConnCount = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP

PKINIT TGT request for a Domain Controller computer account (Certighost forged-cert auth) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the authentication stage of Certighost: a certificate-based (PKINIT) Kerberos TGT request where the target principal is a computer account, i.e. the attacker authenticating as the impersonated Domain Controller using the fraudulently issued certificate. Surfaces the source IP so an analyst can spot a DC$ TGT originating from a non-DC host. Rationale: Article: 'using the certificate to authenticate through PKINIT as the targeted domain controller, saving the resulting Kerberos credentials to a .ccache file.' PreAuthType 16 / populated Certificate Information on a 4768 for a computer account is the PKINIT DC-impersonation tell. Defender/Falcon omitted: DC-side Kerberos ticket events with certificate fields are not shipped in Defender XDR DeviceLogonEvents or Falcon FDR; the authoritative source is DC Security 4768. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/certighost-exploit-lets-low-privileged.html
ATT&CKT1649 T1550.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate smart-card / certificate logon by a service running under a gMSA or computer identity
  • Windows Hello for Business certificate-trust deployments issuing PKINIT logons
  • A genuine domain controller requesting its own TGT via cert-based auth from its own IP
  • Certificate-based device authentication in NDES/SCEP environments
  • Third-party PKI logon appliances performing machine PKINIT
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the SourceIP of the DC$ TGT request against the DC's real IP; a DC computer account getting a PKINIT TGT from a workstation/attacker IP is malicious. Pull the issuing certificate thumbprint and the 4886/4887 that produced it (UC5). 2) Contain: disable the involved certificate (revoke), reset the impersonated DC computer account and, given DCSync risk, plan a double krbtgt reset. 3) Hunt: immediately check for 4662 replication access (UC4) from the same session and any secretsdump-style DCSync activity.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4768   // Kerberos TGT requested
| where TargetUserName endswith "$"   // TGT requested for a computer account (e.g. impersonated DC)
| where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress !in ("::1", "127.0.0.1", "-")
| summarize TgtRequests = count(), SourceIPs = make_set(IpAddress, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by TargetUserName, Computer
| order by LastSeen desc

DCSync (directory replication) requested by a non-DC principal — krbtgt secret theft AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the terminal Certighost objective: DCSync via DRSUAPI GetNCChanges using the impersonated DC's Kerberos credential to pull the krbtgt (and other) secrets. Flags Directory Service Access (4662) requesting the replication extended right by a principal that is not a domain controller. Rationale: Article: 'With the resulting Kerberos credential, the attacker can request account secrets, including the krbtgt secret' via Impacket secretsdump (DCSync). Anchored on the DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All GUID {1131f6ad-...} + domainDNS ObjectType, filtered to non-machine callers. Defender/Falcon omitted: DRSUAPI replication is not surfaced in Defender XDR device tables nor Falcon FDR; the authoritative source is DC Security 4662 (Splunk raw / Sentinel SecurityEvent). CIM has no replication data model, hence raw SPL. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/27/certighost-cve-2026-54121-poc-exploit-released/
ATT&CKT1003.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Azure AD Connect / Entra Connect sync account (MSOL_*) performing legitimate directory replication
  • A newly promoted or additional domain controller replicating (appears with a machine account, already filtered)
  • Third-party backup/PKI tools granted replication rights running under a named service account
  • Password-sync or identity-governance products with delegated Get-Changes rights
  • Security tooling (e.g. BloodHound collectors) legitimately enumerating with a service account
Suppression filter
| where SubjectUserName !startswith "MSOL_" and SubjectUserName !in~ ("svc-aadconnect","svc-adsync")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SubjectUserName; if it is not a DC machine account or a sanctioned sync account (MSOL_/AAD Connect), treat as active DCSync. Check whether the caller recently obtained a DC-impersonation cert (UC5) or PKINIT TGT (UC3). 2) Contain: isolate the requesting host/session, disable the principal, and initiate the emergency krbtgt double-reset plus reset of any secrets pulled. 3) Hunt: enumerate every object the caller replicated, review golden-ticket indicators, and audit AD CS for other DC-account certificate requests.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4662
| where AccessMask == "0x100"   // Control Access (extended right invoked)
| where ObjectType has "19195a5b-6da0-11d0-afd3-00c04fd930c9"   // domainDNS object class
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"   // DCSync from a non-machine principal is anomalous
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("ANONYMOUS LOGON")
| summarize Count = count(), Objects = make_set(ObjectName, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName, Computer
| order by LastSeen desc
title: DCSync Replication Right Requested by Non-DC Principal (Certighost krbtgt Theft)

AD CS certificate request carrying cdc/rmd chase attributes or targeting a DC account (Certighost enrollment) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Certighost enrollment request itself: a certificate request whose attributes include the attacker-controlled cdc (Client DC) and rmd (Remote Domain) chase values, and/or that targets a Domain Controller computer account. These request attributes are the direct fingerprint of the exploit and are otherwise never seen in normal enrollment. Rationale: Article names the two exact request values driving the exploit: 'cdc, or Client DC ... rmd, or Remote Domain' and states the attacker 'submits a certificate request that directs the CA to the rogue services and targets a domain controller account.' Presence of both cdc and rmd in a 4886/4887 Attributes string is a near-zero-FP signature. Sentinel uses the Event table (EventData) because SecurityEvent does not parse the CA Attributes field into a column; Defender/Falcon have no CA enrollment telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/certighost-exploit-lets-low-privileged.html
ATT&CKT1649 T1187
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate certificate requests that coincidentally contain the substrings 'cdc'/'rmd' in a template or SAN (rare; the |all cdc+rmd pairing makes this unlikely)
  • Security testing / red-team validation of the Certighost patch
  • CA request-attribute logging picking up custom enrollment tooling that uses cross-DC hints
  • Backup/restore of CA request rows re-emitting historical events
  • PKI administrators reproducing the PoC in a lab that shares the SIEM
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Attributes/EventData to confirm cdc points to a non-DC host and rmd names a Domain Controller account; identify the Requester principal (correlate to the machine account creator in UC1). 2) Contain: revoke any certificate issued for that request, block the cdc host IP, and apply the July CVE-2026-54121 update or the EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC workaround on the CA. 3) Hunt: check for the follow-on PKINIT DC logon (UC3), certsrv outbound to the cdc host (UC2), and DCSync (UC4); if a cert was issued and used, treat the domain as compromised and reset krbtgt.
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventLog == "Security" or Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing"
| where EventID in (4886, 4887)   // CA received / issued a certificate request
| where EventData has "cdc" and EventData has "rmd"   // attacker chase attributes
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, EventData, RenderedDescription
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
