Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Anubis ransomware execution via distinctive /WIPEMODE /PFAD= /KEY= command-line flags
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anubis ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via hardcoded /for=norealvolume artifact · [LLM] Anubis ransomware mass file encryption — .anubis extension write burst · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anubis ransomware execution via distinctive /WIPEMODE /PFAD= /KEY= command-line flags AIInstallation High
Hunts the Anubis ransomware payload (family that hit Coca-Cola's Fairlife subsidiary) by its unique command-line switch set. Anubis requires operator-supplied flags — /KEY= to start encryption, /elevated to self-escalate, /PFAD= to exclude paths, /PATH= to target a directory, and /WIPEMODE to irreversibly zero files instead of encrypting. The /WIPEMODE and German-language /PFAD= tokens are near-unique to this family. Rationale: Uses the Anubis-specific CLI switches /WIPEMODE, /PFAD= (German 'Pfad'=path), /KEY= and /elevated documented by Trend Micro; /WIPEMODE and /PFAD= are effectively unique to this family, making this very high fidelity even absent hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/anubis-ransomware-adds-wiper-to-destroy-files-beyond-recovery/ • https://blog.barracuda.com/2025/07/11/wipe--leak--extort--the-crazy-hybrid-playbook-of-anubis-ransomwa
ATT&CKT1486 T1485 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup or archival tool that happens to use a /KEY= licensing argument together with an /elevated relaunch flag
  • Custom internal admin scripts that pass a /PATH= directory argument (mitigated — this rule requires /PFAD= or /WIPEMODE specifically)
  • Security-team detonation of Anubis samples in a sandbox/lab host
  • Red-team or purple-team ransomware simulation using the real Anubis binary
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","backup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/WIPEMODE" and ProcessCommandLine !has "/PFAD=")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent process; confirm the binary is unsigned/newly-dropped and check the SHA256 against Trend Micro Anubis IOCs. Note whether /WIPEMODE is present — if so recovery is impossible, treat as destructive. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host immediately via EDR, kill the process tree, and block the binary hash org-wide; alert IR lead given active encryption/wiping. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256/parent across all hosts, look for the paired vssadmin norealvolume shadow-copy deletion and mass .anubis file renames on this and neighbouring hosts, and review recent RDP/WinRM logons to the host for the ingress account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/WIPEMODE","/PFAD=")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "/KEY=" and ProcessCommandLine has "/elevated")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has_any ("/WIPEMODE","/PFAD=")
   or (CommandLine has "/KEY=" and CommandLine has "/elevated")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Anubis Ransomware Command-Line Flags
id: 5b7c1e2a-9f3d-4a1c-8b6e-2d4f7a9c1e30
description: Detects Anubis ransomware payload execution by its distinctive /WIPEMODE, /PFAD= and /KEY=+/elevated command-line switches
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/coca-cola-confirms-data-theft-in-fairlife-ransomware-attack/
  - https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1486
  - attack.t1485
  - attack.t1548
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_wipe:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/WIPEMODE'
      - '/PFAD='
  selection_key:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/KEY='
      - '/elevated'
  condition: selection_wipe or selection_key
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@CommandLine:(*/WIPEMODE* OR */wipemode* OR */WipeMode*) OR @CommandLine:(*/PFAD=* OR */pfad=*) OR (@CommandLine:(*/KEY=* OR */key=*) AND @CommandLine:(*/elevated* OR */ELEVATED*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/\/(WIPEMODE|PFAD=)/i OR (CommandLine=/\/KEY=/i AND CommandLine=/\/elevated/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*/WIPEMODE*" OR Processes.process="*/PFAD=*" OR (Processes.process="*/KEY=*" AND Processes.process="*/elevated*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*/WIPEMODE*" OR Processes.process="*/PFAD=*" OR (Processes.process="*/KEY=*" AND Processes.process="*/elevated*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Anubis ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via hardcoded /for=norealvolume artifact AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Anubis's pre-encryption inhibit-recovery step. The payload shells out 'vssadmin delete shadows /for=norealvolume /all /quiet' — the literal placeholder volume 'norealvolume' is a hardcoded Anubis artifact that distinguishes it from routine vssadmin shadow maintenance. Rationale: The full string 'vssadmin delete shadows /for=norealvolume /all /quiet' is documented by Trend Micro as Anubis's exact shadow-copy deletion command; the bogus 'norealvolume' volume name is a hardcoded artifact absent from any legitimate admin usage, giving near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.securityweek.com/anubis-ransomware-packs-a-wiper-to-permanently-delete-files/
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None realistic for the 'norealvolume' token — it is not a real volume so no legitimate admin or backup product supplies it
  • A malware analyst re-running the Anubis binary in a lab
  • Purple-team ransomware emulation deliberately reproducing the Anubis vssadmin string
  • A YARA/AV signature test harness echoing the command into a log without executing it
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a high-confidence hit — confirm the parent process (the ransomware payload) and its SHA256, and check whether encryption/.anubis renames have already begun on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host via EDR now, kill the parent process tree, and disable the executing account; shadow copies are already gone so prioritise stopping spread over local recovery. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the same parent hash, the /WIPEMODE|/PFAD= command lines, and .anubis file writes; check backup infrastructure and hypervisors (ESXi/Nutanix) for the same actor given Anubis's cross-platform VM targeting.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "delete shadows" and ProcessCommandLine has "norealvolume"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe"
| where CommandLine has "delete shadows" and CommandLine has "norealvolume"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Anubis Ransomware Shadow Copy Deletion (norealvolume artifact)
id: 8e2a6c14-7b93-4d52-a0f1-6c3b9e8d2f47
description: Detects Anubis ransomware inhibiting recovery via vssadmin delete shadows with the hardcoded /for=norealvolume placeholder
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/coca-cola-confirms-data-theft-in-fairlife-ransomware-attack/
  - https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:

detection:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\vssadmin\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/delete\s+shadows/i
| CommandLine=/norealvolume/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Anubis ransomware mass file encryption — .anubis extension write burst AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the impact stage where Anubis appends the .anubis extension to encrypted files (or zeroes them in wiper mode). Aggregates file writes/renames to .anubis per host and process so a single encrypting binary touching many files fires once, not per file. Rationale: Anubis appends the .anubis extension to encrypted files (Trend Micro); a burst of >50 distinct .anubis writes from one process on one host is textbook mass-encryption impact and cleanly distinguishes ransomware from any legitimate single-file usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/anubis-ransomware-group-overview-and-evolution
ATT&CKT1486 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher extracting an Anubis sample set where files are already named *.anubis (mitigated by the >50-distinct-path threshold plus single-process grouping)
  • Backup/AV quarantine that copies encrypted victim files preserving the .anubis name (would show a backup-agent parent, not the ransomware binary)
  • Threat-intel repo sync that writes many .anubis IOC sample files to a security team share
  • DFIR evidence collection copying an encrypted volume onto an analysis host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","msmpeng.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName is an unsigned recently-dropped binary (not a backup or AV agent) and check FileCount trajectory — active climbing count means encryption in progress. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, kill the writing process, block its hash, and snapshot/protect any remaining unencrypted shares and hypervisor datastores. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating SHA256 across the fleet, correlate with the vssadmin norealvolume and /WIPEMODE command-line detections, and check ESXi/Nutanix and NAS telemetry since Anubis encrypts those platforms too.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".anubis"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where FileCount > 50
| order by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".anubis"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileCount > 50
| order by FileCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*.anubis OR *.ANUBIS OR *.Anubis)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.anubis$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=fileCount))
| fileCount > 50
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.anubis" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where distinct_paths > 50
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.anubis" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where distinct_paths > 50
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

Ernst & Young data breach claimed by ShinyHunters extortion gang

BleepingComputer
2026-07-27 6 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

The ShinyHunters extortion gang has claimed responsibility for a recently disclosed Ernst & Young data breach, saying it obtained credentials for some of the company's systems via a supply-chain attack. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1486
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
—
Phase 2
Weaponization
—
Phase 3
Delivery
Detected

Exploitation
Detected

Installation

Likely

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Anomalous first-seen sign-in with valid EY account to GitHub/Azure/Jira (ShinyHunters supply-chain creds)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Single identity authenticating to Jira + GitHub + Azure within one hour (ShinyHunters cross-SaaS credential reuse) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anomalous first-seen sign-in with valid EY account to GitHub/Azure/Jira (ShinyHunters supply-chain creds) AIDelivery Low
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins to the three cloud/SaaS platforms named in the EY breach (GitHub, Azure, Jira/Atlassian) from an ASN or country never before seen for that user in a 30-day baseline. Targets the ShinyHunters technique of authenticating with valid credentials stolen from a compromised upstream supplier rather than exploiting EY directly. Rationale: Anchored on the three environments the article explicitly names as breached (Jira, GitHub, Azure) plus the stated supply-chain valid-account vector; the new-ASN/new-country anti-join against a 30d baseline turns 'valid login' into 'valid login from infrastructure this user has never used', which is the only way to catch stolen-credential reuse absent any IOC. Cross-checked ShinyHunters TTPs (T1078.004/T1199) against EclecticIQ, Microsoft, and Huntress writeups. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/shinyhunters-calling-financially-motivated-data-extortion-group-targeting-enterprise-cloud-applications • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/13/defending-saas-based-applications-against-shinyhunters-oauth-abuse/ • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1199 T1195.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee traveling or on a new mobile carrier/VPN egress producing a first-seen ASN or country
  • New hire's first-ever sign-in to GitHub/Azure/Jira (no baseline exists yet)
  • MSP/consultant legitimately accessing tenant resources from their own corporate ASN
  • Corporate egress IP re-homed to a new ISP/ASN after a network change
  • Cloud-to-cloud service traffic where the user's token is replayed from a datacenter ASN
Suppression filter
| where ClientAppUsed != "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" or UserAgent has_any ("python","curl","Go-http","axios","node-fetch")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the flagged sign-in's IPAddress/ASN/UserAgent and compare to the user's 30-day norm; confirm whether the ASN belongs to a hosting/VPS provider (ShinyHunters commonly egresses from cloud infra) vs a residential/corporate ISP. Check for MFA satisfaction method and any concurrent new MFA-device registration in AuditLogs. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and temporarily block the source IP/ASN via Conditional Access. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every resource that account touched across SigninLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs in the window, look for the same ASN authenticating as other users, and check GitHub/Jira audit logs for bulk repo/ticket reads.
let lookback = 30d;
let recent = 1d;
let SensitiveApps = dynamic(["GitHub","Azure","Windows Azure Service Management","Jira","Atlassian"]);
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize by AccountUpn, Country;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(recent)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ResourceDisplayName has_any (SensitiveApps) or AppDisplayName has_any (SensitiveApps)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn, Country
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
let recent = 1d;
let SensitiveApps = dynamic(["GitHub","Azure","Windows Azure Service Management","Jira","Atlassian"]);
let Baseline = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize by UserPrincipalName, AutonomousSystemNumber;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(recent)
| where ResultType == 0
| where ResourceDisplayName has_any (SensitiveApps) or AppDisplayName has_any (SensitiveApps)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserPrincipalName, AutonomousSystemNumber
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, tostring(Location), AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Single identity authenticating to Jira + GitHub + Azure within one hour (ShinyHunters cross-SaaS credential reuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts one Entra ID identity successfully signing in to two or more of the exact platforms the article says were breached with the same stolen credentials — Jira/Atlassian, GitHub, and Azure — inside a one-hour window. Flags the ShinyHunters pattern of rapidly pivoting a single valid credential set across multiple SaaS/cloud tenants. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's central claim — the same stolen EY credential set breached 'Jira, GitHub, and Azure environments' — as a per-identity fan-out across those exact platform names within a tight window, which is far more specific than a generic impossible-travel rule. ShinyHunters' documented cross-tenant valid-account pivoting (EclecticIQ, Microsoft, Huntress) corroborates the shape. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/shinyhunters-calling-financially-motivated-data-extortion-group-targeting-enterprise-cloud-applications • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/13/defending-saas-based-applications-against-shinyhunters-oauth-abuse/ • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/defending-against-shinyhunters-tactics-and-breaches
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1199 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps/platform engineers who legitimately use GitHub, Azure DevOps and Jira together every hour of the workday
  • CI/CD service or automation accounts federating into all three platforms via SSO
  • A developer's SSO session refreshing tokens for multiple linked apps in one burst
  • Sprint-planning workflows where an engineer opens Jira, a linked GitHub PR, and Azure Portal in sequence
  • Break-glass admin performing a legitimate cross-platform incident review
Suppression filter
| where array_length(SourceIPs) > 1 or array_length(Countries) > 1
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the account is an engineer/DevOps role that normally spans all three platforms (check IdentityInfo Department/JobTitle) — if so, verify all sign-ins share the user's usual IP/ASN. Escalate if the platforms were reached from >1 distinct ASN or a hosting-provider IP. 2) CONTAIN: For an unexplained hit, revoke sessions, reset credentials, and disable any OAuth app consents or new MFA methods added by the account in the window. 3) HUNT: Query GitHub audit log for repo clones/downloads, Jira for bulk issue exports/searches, and Azure activity for resource enumeration by the same principal; pivot on shared source IP to find other affected identities.
let window = 1h;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where PlatformCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
let window = 1h;
SigninLogs

| where PlatformCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:0 @properties.appDisplayName:(*GitHub* OR *Jira* OR *Atlassian* OR *Azure*)

Public Exploit Released for Patched vBulletin Pre-Auth Code Execution Flaw

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 8 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Public exploit details released on July 27 show how an unauthenticated request can reach PHP's eval() function inside vBulletin and execute code on an unpatched forum server. The attack requires no account, administrative access, or interaction from another user. SSD Secure Disclosure lists vBulletin 6.2.1 and earlier, and 6.1.6 and earlier, as affected, but does not give a lower version

vBulletin CVE-2026-61511 pre-auth RCE via operator-laden pagenav[pagenumber] to ajax/render/pagenav AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to vBulletin's public template-render route ajax/render/pagenav where the pagenav[pagenumber] parameter — normally a plain integer — carries parentheses, XOR/OR/NOT operators or concatenation characters. This is the exact 'phpfuck' restricted-character payload SSD's PoC feeds into vB5_Template_Runtime::runMaths() and PHP eval() for unauthenticated code execution. Rationale: pagenav[pagenumber] legitimately only ever holds an integer, so any parenthesis, XOR (^/%5e), OR (|/%7c), NOT (~/%7e) or concatenation character in it on the ajax/render/pagenav route is the phpfuck eval payload from SSD's PoC — near-zero legitimate overlap. Corroborated against SSD's technical advisory and independent write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://gbhackers.com/vbulletin-pre-auth-rce-flaw/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vbulletin-flaw-execute-php-code/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners/pentest tools (Acunetix, Nuclei) firing the same CVE-2026-61511 template against your own forum
  • Internal vulnerability-management authenticated scans replaying the PoC
  • A plugin or theme that legitimately passes non-numeric pagenav values (rare — verify against a known-good baseline)
  • WAF in monitor-only mode logging blocked attempts that never reached PHP
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the endpoint from known IPs
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction !in ("blocked","deny","Blocked") and SourceIP !in ("")   // keep allowed requests; append known scanner IPs to the exclusion list
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestURL/body and SourceIP; URL-decode the pagenav[pagenumber] value and confirm it reconstructs PHP tokens (parentheses + ^ + digits, no letters). Check whether the WAF blocked or allowed (DeviceAction) and the HTTP response code. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, and confirm the forum is on vBulletin 6.2.2 (or branch patch for 6.2.1/6.2.0/6.1.6) — if not, take it offline or virtual-patch the ajax/render/pagenav route immediately. 3) Hunt: on the web host run the companion 'web-server spawns shell' detection to see if system() executed, review file writes under the webroot for dropped PHP web shells, and search all historical logs for the same SourceIP and payload signature.

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vBulletin web-server process (php-fpm/httpd/w3wp) spawning OS shell — CVE-2026-61511 post-exploitation AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the vBulletin/PHP web-server process spawning a command interpreter or recon binary, which is exactly what SSD's PoC does after rebuilding PHP's system() to run an OS command and return output in the HTTP response. A php-fpm/httpd/w3wp parent launching cmd/powershell/bash/curl/whoami is not normal forum behaviour. Rationale: A php-fpm/httpd/w3wp/nginx parent process spawning cmd/powershell/bash/curl/whoami is the direct on-host artefact of the runMaths()->eval()->system() chain described by SSD; forum servers effectively never legitimately shell out from the web worker. Parent+child pairing keeps FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://gbhackers.com/vbulletin-pre-auth-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PHP plugins that shell out (image processing via ImageMagick/convert, cron-like maintenance tasks)
  • Server admins running interactive troubleshooting under the web service account
  • Deployment/CI scripts invoking curl or git from the web root during releases
  • Monitoring agents that exec whoami/uname under the httpd context
  • Backup jobs spawned by the web user
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("convert","ImageMagick","git pull","/usr/local/bin/backup")   // drop known benign image/maintenance shell-outs; tune per environment
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain; benign maintenance has predictable args (image resize, git pull) whereas exploitation shows recon (whoami/id/uname) or outbound curl/wget to unknown hosts. Correlate the timestamp with the web-log detection's SourceIP hitting ajax/render/pagenav. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, and rotate any DB/API credentials readable from the vBulletin config. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the web user under the webroot for PHP web shells, review outbound connections from the web-server process, and confirm patch level is 6.2.2.

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","curl","curl.exe","wget","whoami","whoami.exe","id","uname","python","python3")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256

Unpatched vBulletin instances exposed to CVE-2026-61511 AIReconnaissance Medium
Audit hunt surfacing managed hosts running vBulletin below the fixed 6.2.2 release (affected: 6.2.1 and earlier, 6.1.6 and earlier). Given a public exploit is live and the fix predates disclosure by ~4 weeks, this identifies the concentrated self-hosted, internet-facing population still exploitable. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete CVE id CVE-2026-61511 and the vendor's fixed version 6.2.2 versus affected 6.2.1/6.1.6-and-earlier stated in the article and SSD advisory; joining IsInternetFacing prioritises the exact exploitable population the article flags. If TVM has not yet mapped the CVE, fall back to DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory where SoftwareName has 'vbulletin' and SoftwareVersion != '6.2.2'. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://gbhackers.com/vbulletin-pre-auth-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to 6.2.2 but TVM inventory lagging its scan refresh
  • Development/staging forum clones not reachable from the internet (lower priority, not false — still vulnerable)
  • vBulletin Cloud-managed sites reported already patched by the vendor
  • Version string parsed from a customised/rebranded footer that misreports the build
  • Decommissioned hosts still in the TVM inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort results by IsInternetFacing to prioritise externally reachable forums; confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely below 6.2.2 (or a branch patch for 6.2.1/6.2.0/6.1.6). 2) Contain: schedule emergency upgrade to 6.2.2 or apply the branch patch; where patching is delayed, virtual-patch or block the ajax/render/pagenav route at the WAF. 3) Hunt: for each unpatched internet-facing host, run the web-log payload detection and the web-server-spawns-shell detection over the full ~4-week exposure window (late-June patch to July-27 disclosure) to check for prior compromise.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

n8n Sandbox Escape Lets Workflow Editors Run OS Commands as the n8n Process

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 10 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

n8n has patched a high-severity expression-sandbox escape that could let an authenticated workflow editor execute operating-system commands on the server running the automation platform. Security Joes found the flaw while probing n8n's February fix for CVE-2026-27577 for another bypass. The affected ranges are &lt;2.31.5 and &gt;=2.32.0,&lt;2.32.1. n8n fixed the flaw in versions 2.31.5 and

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] n8n/Node.js process spawning shell or recon utility (sandbox-escape RCE) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — n8n Sandbox Escape Lets Workflow Editors Run OS Commands as the n8n Process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] curl/wget/nc spawned by n8n/Node reaching external hosts (post-escape C2/exfil)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] n8n/Node child command accessing N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY or host credential stores
n8n/Node.js process spawning shell or recon utility (sandbox-escape RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the direct observable of the n8n expression-sandbox escape (GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m): the n8n/Node process loading child_process and executing OS commands, surfacing as a shell (sh/bash/cmd/powershell) or recon utility (whoami/id/curl) spawned as a child of node/n8n. This is exactly the parent→child chain the advisory tells defenders to hunt. Rationale: Anchored on the advisory's explicit hunt guidance ('shells, PowerShell, curl, or wget spawned as children of the n8n or Node.js process') and the child_process load in the exploit chain; parent=node/n8n + shell/recon child is the escape's only host-level footprint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vpcf-gvg4-6qwr
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate n8n Execute Command node running sh/bash by design
  • Node-based CI runners or container entrypoints invoking bash/sh
  • Health-check workflows calling curl/wget to internal APIs
  • Admin debugging inside the n8n container (id/whoami)
  • Task-runner or npm lifecycle scripts spawning shell wrappers
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("n8n-nodes-base.executeCommand","/opt/n8n/healthcheck") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and the initiating node/n8n cmdline; confirm whether an Execute Command node exists in the workflow that ran, and identify the workflow author. 2) Contain: if the command is unexpected (recon, encryption-key read, outbound tooling), isolate the host and suspend the n8n workflow-editor account that authored/last-modified the workflow. 3) Hunt: review recently created/modified workflows for arrow functions or obfuscated JS, pivot on the same host for outbound connections and N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY access; rotate n8n credentials and the encryption key.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","n8n") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","n8n")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","csh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","whoami","id","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","python","python3","perl","ruby")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","n8n") or ParentProcessName has_any ("node","n8n")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/csh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","/pwsh","pwsh.exe","/whoami","/id","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/netcat","/python","/perl","/ruby")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: n8n Node.js Process Spawning Shell or Recon Utility (Sandbox Escape)
id: 3c9d1e6a-8b42-4f21-9d7a-1f2b6c4e8a01
status: experimental
description: Detects n8n/Node.js spawning a command interpreter or recon utility, the direct observable of the n8n expression-sandbox escape GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m (child_process RCE).
references:
  - https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/n8n-sandbox-escape-lets-workflow.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.t1203
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/node'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '/n8n'
  child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/ksh'
      - '/csh'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '/pwsh'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '/whoami'
      - '/id'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/netcat'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/perl'
      - '/ruby'
  condition: parent and child
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate n8n Execute Command node usage
  - CI/CD or container entrypoint scripts launched by node
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\n8n.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\whoami.exe OR *\\nc.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|n8n)(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/[\/\\](sh|bash|dash|zsh|ksh|csh|cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh|whoami|id|curl|wget|nc|ncat|netcat|python3?|perl|ruby)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","n8n")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","csh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","whoami","id","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","python","python3","perl","ruby")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","n8n")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","csh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","whoami","id","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","python","python3","perl","ruby")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
curl/wget/nc spawned by n8n/Node reaching external hosts (post-escape C2/exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network egress originating from a download/transfer utility (curl, wget, nc, python) whose parent is the n8n/Node process — the payload-fetch or exfil step after the sandbox escape. Distinct from the process-spawn UC by pivoting on the outbound public connection rather than the spawn event. Rationale: The advisory names curl/wget as children to hunt, and Security Joes notes the escape opens 'paths to connected databases, internal services, and cloud endpoints' — a transfer utility parented by node reaching a public IP is the payload-fetch/exfil observable. Sentinel/Splunk express it via process telemetry since ASIM/CIM network events aren't parent-attributed. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/n8n-sandbox-escape-lets-workflow.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • n8n HTTP Request node internally shelling out to curl for an integration
  • Workflow that legitimately fetches files from a public API via curl/wget
  • Python-based custom n8n node calling external SaaS endpoints
  • Container image pulls or update scripts run under the node parent
  • Monitoring/health probes to external status pages
Suppression filter
| where RemotePort in (4444,5555,6666,7777,8888,9999) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and the utility's full command line; check whether the destination matches a known integration endpoint for that workflow. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress and isolate the host if the destination is unrecognized or the transfer is credential-bearing. 3) Hunt: correlate to the process-spawn UC on the same host/time, review the responsible workflow for arrow-function/obfuscated JS, and rotate any credentials reachable from the n8n host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","n8n")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","bash","sh","python","python3","perl")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","n8n") or ParentProcessName has_any ("node","n8n")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/netcat","/python","/perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\nc.exe OR *\\powershell.exe) NOT (CIDR(@DestinationIp, 10.0.0.0/8) OR CIDR(@DestinationIp, 172.16.0.0/12) OR CIDR(@DestinationIp, 192.168.0.0/16))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/[\/\\](curl|wget|nc|ncat|netcat|bash|sh|python3?|perl)$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","n8n")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","bash","sh","python","python3","perl")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","n8n")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","bash","sh","python","python3","perl")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
n8n/Node child command accessing N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY or host credential stores AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts commands spawned under the n8n/Node process that read the n8n encryption key, host secret files (/etc/shadow, SSH keys, cloud creds) or dump the environment — the credential-theft objective Security Joes flagged (exposing N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY to decrypt stored credentials). Pivots on command-line content rather than the child binary name. Rationale: Directly anchored on Security Joes' finding that the escape 'could expose N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY and allow decryption of credentials stored in n8n'; a node-parented command touching that key or host secret files is high-fidelity credential access with almost no benign analogue. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/n8n-sandbox-escape-lets-workflow.html
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • n8n startup legitimately reading its own .n8n/config file
  • Container init reading /proc/self/environ for config bootstrap
  • Admin running printenv inside the n8n container for troubleshooting
  • Backup jobs archiving the .n8n directory
  • Legit workflow that references an SSH key path for an SFTP integration
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has ".n8n/config" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "n8n start")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child command line and confirm whether it reads N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY or host secrets outside n8n's normal config load; identify the workflow and its author. 2) Contain: treat the encryption key and all n8n-stored credentials as compromised — rotate the key and every stored credential, and disable the responsible workflow-editor account. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound connections from the host (exfil of the harvested secrets), review connected databases/cloud endpoints for the n8n service identity's activity, and audit other recently modified workflows for arrow-function/obfuscated JS.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","n8n") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","n8n")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY","/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","id_rsa",".aws/credentials",".n8n/config","printenv","/proc/self/environ",".ssh/","/root/.n8n")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","n8n") or ParentProcessName has_any ("node","n8n")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY","/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","id_rsa",".aws/credentials",".n8n/config","printenv","/proc/self/environ",".ssh/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 8a41f7c2-2d95-4b6e-9c1a-7e0b3d5f4c22

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-27577")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-27577")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Exploitation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Operation BlueDash fake Teams/Zoom update payload-host infrastructure contact AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint contact to the counterfeit Microsoft Store / GitHub Pages infrastructure used by Operation BlueDash to serve the fake Teams update and the supportdev.exe loader. These are hard campaign IOCs (teamvem.com, support.berrydev.xyz, berry4603.github.io) rather than generic phishing domains. Rationale: Uses the three confirmed BlueDash hostnames from the article body (teamvem.com fake Teams store page, support.berrydev.xyz actor infra, berry4603.github.io repo host) plus the pre-extracted anuyotindustries.com. Domain-exact matches make this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/03/signed-malware-impersonating-workplace-apps-deploys-rmm-backdoors/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/phishing-rmm-tools/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox reaching the live domain
  • Proxy/DNS sinkhole appliance pre-resolving IOC lists for blocking
  • github.io is shared infrastructure — only berry4603.github.io is malicious, a typo/partial match could catch other github.io if the has_any list is widened
  • Corporate phishing-simulation vendor mimicking the lure
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which host/user resolved the domain and whether supportdev.exe was subsequently written or executed (pivot to UC2). 2) Contain: block all four domains at proxy/DNS, isolate the host if a download or process launch followed the DNS hit. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for supportdev.exe file writes and any process command line containing LEVEL_API_KEY (UC3) or ScreenConnect/Tactical RMM installers landing in %TEMP%.

supportdev.exe Inno Setup loader spawning hidden-window PowerShell AIInstallation High
Detects the BlueDash first-stage loader supportdev.exe launching PowerShell in a hidden window to fetch and enroll RMM agents. The parent binary name plus the hidden-window child is the article's specific execution fingerprint. Rationale: supportdev.exe is the named Inno Setup loader from the article; pairing its unusual parent role with a hidden PowerShell child that pulls RMM installers is the exact execution behaviour ZeroBEC described. Parent-name match alone is near-unique. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/operation-bluedash-deploys-level-rmm.html • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/phishing-rmm-tools/

  • EDR/AV sandbox replay of the sample generating benign telemetry
  • IT deployment script legitimately named support*.exe (widen-match risk if endswith is loosened)

Level RMM enrollment with BlueDash attacker API key (GxSCHE8EZwfyYN3iPQHPai8D) AIInstallation High
Highest-fidelity BlueDash indicator: any process command line carrying the attacker-controlled Level RMM enrollment secret. A single hit means an endpoint was silently enrolled into the actor's Level RMM tenant. Rationale: GxSCHE8EZwfyYN3iPQHPai8D is the verbatim LEVEL_API_KEY enrollment secret quoted in the article; it is a fixed, unique string that will not appear in any legitimate enrollment, so a match is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/operation-bluedash-deploys-level-rmm.html
ATT&CKT1219 T1608
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Detection-engineering test data or purple-team exercise deliberately replaying the IOC
  • Threat-intel platform indexing the article text into a ticketing/command-execution context
  • No realistic benign scenario produces this exact 24-char secret
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is now enrolled in an unknown Level RMM tenant — check for the Level agent service/binary and outbound Level.io C2. 2) Contain: isolate the host, uninstall/kill the Level agent, revoke the enrollment, and reset the logged-on user's credentials. 3) Hunt: this key implies parallel ScreenConnect/Tactical RMM drops — run UC4 (co-resident RMM) and UC5 (RMM-context recon) across the estate and block Level enrollment egress if RMM isn't sanctioned.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "GxSCHE8EZwfyYN3iPQHPai8D" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "GxSCHE8EZwfyYN3iPQHPai8D"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "GxSCHE8EZwfyYN3iPQHPai8D"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Multiple RMM agents co-resident on one host (BlueDash redundant access) AIInstallation Medium
Detects two or more distinct RMM families (ScreenConnect + Level + Tactical RMM/MeshAgent) appearing on the same endpoint within a short window — the BlueDash resilience pattern of stacking RMM tools so removal of one leaves access intact. Rationale: The article explicitly states Level RMM + ConnectWise ScreenConnect are dropped in parallel and a sibling repo adds Tactical RMM, framed as deliberate redundant access. Counting distinct RMM families per host targets that stacking behaviour rather than any single tool, which alone can be legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/03/signed-malware-impersonating-workplace-apps-deploys-rmm-backdoors/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/phishing-rmm-tools/
ATT&CKT1219 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP migrating a client from one RMM (e.g. ScreenConnect) to another (e.g. Tactical RMM) leaving both temporarily installed
  • Sanctioned IT stack that genuinely runs two RMM/remote-support tools
  • MeshAgent bundled by Tactical RMM counted as a separate family (tune the family mapping)
  • Security tooling that embeds a MeshAgent-derived component
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic([]))  // add sanctioned dual-RMM hosts / MSP-migration assets to this allowlist
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether both RMM families are sanctioned for this host — check asset inventory and the installing parent process (unsigned/%TEMP% install = malicious). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate, uninstall all rogue agents, and block their C2/enrollment endpoints. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 for the Level enrollment key and UC5 for recon commands run through the RMM context; check other hosts touched by the same installing user.
let RmmBins = dynamic(["screenconnect.clientservice.exe","screenconnect.windowsclient.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","meshagent.exe","level.exe","level-windows-amd64.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| extend fn = tolower(FileName)
| where fn in (RmmBins) or ProcessCommandLine has "LEVEL_API_KEY"
| extend RmmFamily = case(
    fn startswith "screenconnect", "ScreenConnect",
    fn in ("tacticalrmm.exe","meshagent.exe"), "TacticalRMM",
    fn startswith "level" or ProcessCommandLine has "LEVEL_API_KEY", "LevelRMM",
    "Other")
| summarize Families = make_set(RmmFamily), FamilyCount = dcount(RmmFamily), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 5) by DeviceName
| where FamilyCount >= 2   // 2+ distinct RMM families on one host = redundant-access pattern
| order by LastSeen desc

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe OR *\screenconnect.clientservice.exe OR *\ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe OR *\tacticalrmm.exe OR *\TacticalRMM.exe OR *\meshagent.exe OR *\MeshAgent.exe OR *\level.exe OR *\Level.exe) OR @CommandLine:*LEVEL_API_KEY*)

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=collect([fam]))
| famcount:=count(fam, distinct=true, as=famcount)

Host reconnaissance sequence spawned from an RMM agent context (BlueDash operator checklist) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the BlueDash post-install discovery checklist — reboot-pending check, BitLocker/system-volume status, firewall-profile enumeration and local Administrators enumeration — when the parent process is an RMM agent rather than an approved IT workflow. This is the behavioural opportunity ZeroBEC highlighted. Rationale: Maps the article's explicit operator checklist (reboot-pending, system-volume/BitLocker protection, firewall profiles, local Administrators membership) to their canonical Windows commands, gated on an RMM parent — the exact 'unauthorized RMM context vs approved IT workflow' distinction ZeroBEC called out as the detection opportunity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/operation-bluedash-deploys-level-rmm.html • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/phishing-rmm-tools/
ATT&CKT1069.001 T1518.001 T1082 T1016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned MSP running the same triage commands via ScreenConnect/Tactical RMM during legitimate support
  • Automated RMM monitoring scripts polling BitLocker or firewall status as health checks
  • Patch-readiness tooling checking PendingFileRenameOperations before reboot
  • Helpdesk technician enumerating local admins to fix a user permission issue
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and DeviceName !in~ (dynamic([]))  // allowlist sanctioned MSP/RMM-managed hosts here
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the RMM agent itself is sanctioned (cross-check UC4); if the agent is rogue, every child command is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the RMM session, and preserve the process tree for the operator command sequence. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on privilege escalation or lateral movement from the same session and confirm whether the recon preceded additional payload staging or account manipulation.
let RmmParents = dynamic(["screenconnect.clientservice.exe","screenconnect.windowsclient.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","meshagent.exe","level.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) in (RmmParents)
| extend Cmd = tolower(ProcessCommandLine)
| where (FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe") and Cmd has "localgroup" and Cmd has "admin")
    or (FileName =~ "manage-bde.exe" and Cmd has "-status")
    or (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and Cmd has_all ("advfirewall","show"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and Cmd has_any ("get-bitlockervolume","get-localgroupmember","pendingfilerenameoperations","win32_shadowcopy","netfirewallprofile"))
| summarize Recon = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), ReconTypes = dcount(FileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
let RmmParents = dynamic(["screenconnect.clientservice.exe","screenconnect.windowsclient.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","meshagent.exe","level.exe"]);
SecurityEvent

| extend cfn = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
