Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

      article before alerting.
level: medium

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Phishing email from npm-lookalike domain npmjs.help AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail sent from, or containing links to, the npmjs.help lookalike domain used to phish npm maintainers ('qix'/chalk-debug campaign) into surrendering 2FA/credentials on a fake npm support portal. Article-specific: npmjs.help is a typosquat of the legitimate npmjs.com and has no benign use. Rationale: Uses the exact IOC npmjs.help; a corroborated typosquat of npmjs.com used to send support@npmjs.help phishing to npm maintainers — any inbound mail from it or containing its URLs is malicious with near-zero legitimate traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/20-popular-npm-packages-compromised-chalk-debug-strip-ansi-color-convert-wrap-ansi • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/chalk-and-17-other-npm-packages-compromised-in-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness team forwarding a captured phishing sample internally for training
  • Threat-intel analyst emailing the IOC domain string in the body of a report (matched by the Recipients/body has-clause)
  • A quarantined message surfacing in a defender/SOC review mailbox rather than a real inbox delivery
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryLocation !in ("Quarantine","Blocked") or isempty(DeliveryLocation)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation for each hit — anything Delivered/Inbox to a live user is priority; identify recipients who are package maintainers or have npm/PyPI publishing rights. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message org-wide (Explorer or Search-and-Purge), block npmjs.help at the mail gateway and web proxy, and force credential + npm/PyPI token reset for any recipient who interacted. 3) Hunt: check UrlClickEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents for anyone who reached npmjs.help (see companion UC), and review recent package publishes / token creations from those maintainer accounts.
let win = 30d;
let bad = dynamic(["npmjs.help"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(win)
| where SenderFromDomain in~ (bad) or SenderMailFromDomain in~ (bad)
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, ThreatTypes
| union (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(win)
    | where UrlDomain in~ (bad)
    | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let win = 30d;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(win)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Sender endswith "npmjs.help" or P2Sender endswith "npmjs.help" or tostring(Recipients) has "npmjs.help"
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, Sender, P2Sender, Recipients, Subject, MailboxOwnerUPN, ClientIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Endpoint DNS/HTTP connection to npm-phish portal npmjs.help AIExploitation High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to npmjs.help — the fake npm support/2FA portal from the chalk-debug maintainer-phishing campaign. A hit means a user reached the credential-harvesting site, the step immediately preceding npm account takeover and malicious package publication. Rationale: Matches the exact corroborated IOC npmjs.help at the DNS/HTTP layer; the domain is a typosquat with no legitimate destination, so any endpoint reaching it is a maintainer interacting with the credential-harvest portal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/20-popular-npm-packages-compromised-chalk-debug-strip-ansi-color-convert-wrap-ansi
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst manually browsing to npmjs.help during IOC verification/sandboxing
  • Secure web gateway or URL-detonation sandbox pre-fetching the link from a quarantined email
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion tool performing passive DNS enrichment on the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, user, and InitiatingProcess — a real browser (chrome/msedge/firefox) reaching npmjs.help from a maintainer workstation is high severity; a proxy/sandbox appliance is likely benign. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block npmjs.help at DNS and proxy, isolate the host if a browser hit is confirmed, and immediately rotate the user's npm/PyPI credentials, session tokens, and publish/automation tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate with the companion email UC for the delivering message, and review that maintainer's npm/PyPI account for new tokens, 2FA changes, or package versions published in the following days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npmjs.help"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let win = 30d;
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(win) | where Name has "npmjs.help" | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, Client=ClientIP, Query=Name, QueryType),
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(win) | where DnsQuery has "npmjs.help" | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, Client=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryType),
(ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(win) | where Url has "npmjs.help" | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, Client=SrcIpAddr, Query=Url)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Steam forum ClickFix attacks infect gamers with XMRig cryptominers
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Microsoft Defender path exclusion added for C:\Windows\Background (ClickFix XMRig) · [LLM] Scheduled task 'XMRig-<host>' launching C:\Windows\Background\system.exe as SYSTEM · [LLM] Payload written to C:\Windows\Background\system.exe (XMRig drop) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection / DNS to msfconfig.icu (XMRig payload download) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] XMRig miner executing as SYSTEM from C:\Windows\Background
Microsoft Defender path exclusion added for C:\Windows\Background (ClickFix XMRig) AIInstallation High
Hunts the ClickFix/msf-utility campaign registering C:\Windows\Background as a Defender scan exclusion before dropping system.exe. Legitimate software almost never excludes a folder directly under C:\Windows, making the exclusion path itself high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchors on the exact defense-evasion artifact from the article — a Defender exclusion for C:\Windows\Background — which is a fixed, campaign-specific path. Corroborated by TechEchelon and daily.dev write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise EDR/AV migration scripts that add temporary exclusions during agent installs
  • Backup or imaging software that legitimately excludes a staging folder (rarely under C:\Windows though)
  • Sysadmin manually running Add-MpPreference during troubleshooting (would not target C:\Windows\Background)
  • In-house build/CI tooling excluding artifact directories
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and RegistryValueData !has @"C:\Windows\Background")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): On the alerting host, run Get-MpPreference to confirm C:\Windows\Background is an active exclusion and check whether the folder and system.exe exist. Identify the initiating account/process. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate the host, remove the exclusion (Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath 'C:\Windows\Background'), then delete the XMRig scheduled task and the folder. Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot on the same host and org for outbound traffic to msfconfig.icu, a scheduled task named XMRig-*, and other hosts with the same exclusion path.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValueName has "Background" or RegistryValueData has @"C:\Windows\Background"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValue has "Background" or RegistryValueData has @"C:\Windows\Background"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task 'XMRig-<host>' launching C:\Windows\Background\system.exe as SYSTEM AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the campaign's persistence mechanism: a scheduled task prefixed 'XMRig-' that runs system.exe from C:\Windows\Background with SYSTEM privileges at every boot. The task name prefix and target path are both hardcoded and campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the two hardcoded campaign strings — task-name prefix 'XMRig-' and target binary C:\Windows\Background\system.exe — so it fires only on this specific persistence, not generic schtasks usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1496
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin task named with 'XMRig' during malware-removal/testing
  • Security researcher reproducing the sample in a lab
  • EDR remediation script that recreates then deletes the task to clean it
  • None expected in normal enterprise operation — the path C:\Windows\Background is non-standard
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SenseIR.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "/delete")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Run schtasks /query /tn XMRig-<hostname> /v and confirm the action points to C:\Windows\Background\system.exe and runs as SYSTEM. Note the creating account and time. Step 2 (Contain): Delete the task (schtasks /delete /tn XMRig-<hostname> /f), kill running system.exe/xmrig processes, isolate host. Step 3 (Hunt): Check the same host for the Defender exclusion and msfconfig.icu connections; sweep the fleet for any XMRig-* task or system.exe under C:\Windows\Background.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "XMRig-" or ProcessCommandLine has @"C:\Windows\Background\system.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe" or CommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask"
| where CommandLine has "XMRig-" or CommandLine has @"\Windows\Background\system.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection / DNS to msfconfig.icu (XMRig payload download) AICommand & Control High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the campaign C2 msfconfig.icu, from which the XMRig payload is pulled over TCP/443 at /tmp/system.txt. The domain is a dedicated attacker-controlled indicator with no legitimate use. Rationale: msfconfig.icu is a dedicated attacker domain confirmed by multiple write-ups; any resolution or connection to it (or a fetch of /tmp/system.txt) is a direct hit with essentially no benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers • https://daily.dev/posts/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers-keosw3y2g
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst or sandbox detonating the sample and resolving the domain
  • Security tool actively probing/sinkholing the IOC
  • DNS security appliance logging a blocked-but-attempted lookup (still worth reviewing)
  • No benign business use of a .icu 'msfconfig' domain is expected
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Identify which process on the host initiated the lookup/connection (expect powershell.exe) and whether a file was written to C:\Windows\Background afterward. Step 2 (Contain): Block msfconfig.icu at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and remove the temporary firewall allow-rule the script created. Step 3 (Hunt): Sweep DNS/proxy logs org-wide for msfconfig.icu, and on any matching host look for system.exe, the XMRig-* task, and the Defender exclusion.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "msfconfig.icu" or RemoteUrl endswith "/tmp/system.txt"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery =~ "msfconfig.icu" or DnsQuery endswith ".msfconfig.icu"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Payload written to C:\Windows\Background\system.exe (XMRig drop) AIInstallation High
Hunts the file-write of the downloaded XMRig payload to the campaign's fixed install directory C:\Windows\Background. This directory is created by the malware and is not a legitimate Windows path, so any executable written there is suspicious. Rationale: C:\Windows\Background is a fixed, malware-created directory named explicitly in the article; any file write there (system.exe or config.json) is a durable install-stage indicator distinct from the network and persistence pivots. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Backup software re-writing the folder during recovery testing
  • No legitimate Windows component writes to C:\Windows\Background
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Hash system.exe and submit to your sandbox/VT; confirm it is XMRig and capture FileOriginUrl (expect msfconfig.icu). Identify the writing process. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate host, stop/kill xmrig and system processes, delete C:\Windows\Background and its contents after preserving a sample. Step 3 (Hunt): Correlate with the XMRig-* scheduled task, the Defender exclusion, and msfconfig.icu traffic on this and other hosts.

XMRig miner executing as SYSTEM from C:\Windows\Background AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of the miner itself — a process running from C:\Windows\Background (system.exe, or a process masquerading as 'system'/'xmrig') typically launched by the scheduler at SYSTEM integrity. This catches the resource-hijacking stage even if the drop/persistence events were missed. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact execution artifact — a binary named system.exe/xmrig.exe running out of C:\Windows\Background — a masqueraded location + name that no legitimate Windows process uses, catching the impact stage independently of the drop. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-forum-clickfix-attacks-infect-gamers-with-xmrig-cryptominers/ • https://www.techechelon.com/post/steam-forums-weaponized-in-clickfix-campaign-distributing-xmrig-cryptominers

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • No benign software ships a system.exe/xmrig.exe under C:\Windows\Background
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Confirm the parent is a scheduler/svchost (SYSTEM launch) and check CPU utilisation; hash the image to confirm XMRig. Step 2 (Contain): Kill the process tree, disable/delete the XMRig-* task, isolate the host, and remove C:\Windows\Background plus the Defender exclusion. Step 3 (Hunt): Look for msfconfig.icu beaconing/pool traffic and enumerate other hosts running system.exe from C:\Windows\Background or holding the XMRig-* task.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Malvertising Sends Malware in Pieces, Then Makes the Browser Build the Executable

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 16 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malvertising operation dubbed SourTrade is making victims' browsers build the final Windows executable themselves, using a legitimate Bun runtime as its base instead of serving one complete malicious file from a fixed URL. Exploitation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

SourTrade malvertising infrastructure contact (campaign domains + Bun-runtime host) AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS resolution / network connections to the published SourTrade landing-page and secondary-runtime domains, including purelogicbox.org which serves the clean Bun runtime. This is the delivery-infrastructure IOC pivot for the browser-assembled malware campaign detailed by Confiant. Rationale: Uses the concrete SourTrade domain IOCs published by Confiant and re-counted by The Hacker News (purelogicbox.org is specifically the Bun-runtime host). Domain-list resolution from a browser is high-fidelity because these are single-purpose malvertising domains with no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-sites-use-javascript-to-build-malware-in-browser-memory/
ATT&CKT1189 T1583.008
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonating a SourTrade sample intentionally
  • Threat-intel platform or URL-scanning appliance crawling the IOC domains
  • A future benign re-registration of an expired campaign domain (domains rotate)
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS logging the block as a query event
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MonitoringHost.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("sandbox-detonation-host")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved the domain and the initiating browser process; check whether a same-session .exe download landed in Downloads (pivot to UC2). 2) Contain: block the domain(s) at the DNS/proxy layer, isolate the host if an executable was written, and reset any trading/wallet credentials the user may have entered on the fake landing page. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the full 96-domain SourTrade set, look for browser-written .exe files with FileOriginUrl on any campaign domain, and review ad-referral chains that led the user to the landing page.

Browser-assembled SourTrade executable dropped with campaign-domain origin (MotW) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a browser process writing a .exe to disk whose Mark-of-the-Web download source (FileOriginUrl/ReferrerUrl) is a SourTrade landing-page domain, plus the three published sample hashes. This is the article-specific moment the in-browser-assembled Bun executable lands on disk — the point where per-session hash rotation is defeated by pivoting on origin rather than hash. Rationale: The Defender query pivots on FileOriginUrl/ReferrerUrl — the MotW record Confiant notes points at the landing page domain, not the Bun-runtime host — which survives the per-session hash rotation the campaign relies on. The three published SHA-256 samples are added as a direct fallback; Splunk/Falcon fall back to browser-written .exe in Downloads because CIM/FDR lack an origin-URL field. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://gbhackers.com/sourtrade-browser-assembled/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html
ATT&CKT1027 T1105 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers downloaded via browser to Downloads (very common on the hash-less fallback branch)
  • Portable apps or dev tools (e.g. genuine Bun/Node installers) saved by developers
  • Browser auto-update stub executables written to profile folders
  • Corporate software-portal downloads delivering signed .exe installers
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe") and isempty(FileOriginUrl) and isempty(FileOriginReferrerUrl) and SHA256 !in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b","05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6","ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FileOriginUrl/ReferrerUrl resolves to a SourTrade domain (high-confidence branch) or that the .exe is unsigned/low-prevalence on the Downloads fallback branch; check the process tree for subsequent execution. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the origin domain, and isolate the host if the executable ran; because JSCEAL/WeevilProxy is the likely payload, treat as credential-theft — force-reset the user's trading, wallet, and SSO credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot the origin domain into UC1/UC3, look for a same-origin ServiceWorker /config fetch preceding the write, and scan for Bun-runtime standalone executables launched from Downloads across the fleet.

SourTrade ServiceWorker build-instruction fetch (/config + /sw.js on campaign domains) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts web-proxy requests to the /sw.js ServiceWorker and /config build-instruction endpoints on SourTrade campaign domains — the exact same-origin paths the landing page uses to register the worker and pull the PE header, section table, .bun bytecode and secondary runtime URL. Scoped to the campaign domains, this catches the technique even as individual sample hashes rotate and helps surface newly-registered domains reusing the pattern. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim /sw.js and /config paths (article code blocks) scoped to the confirmed campaign domains — the ServiceWorker + build-instruction pattern is the campaign's signature and survives hash rotation. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because FDR and the available Datadog sources do not carry URL request paths and there is no AWS telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://cybersecuritynews.com/sourtrade-malvertising-malware/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1189
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A future benign re-registration of an expired SourTrade domain serving a legitimate /config or /sw.js
  • Proxy logging a blocked request as an allowed event after policy change
  • Security scanner / crawler fetching the campaign paths during investigation
  • Rare legitimate PWA on a re-purposed domain registering a service worker at /sw.js
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host+user made the /config fetch and whether a /sw.js registration and secondary purelogicbox.org runtime fetch occurred in the same session; check for a subsequent browser-written .exe (UC2). 2) Contain: block the domain at the proxy, clear the browser's registered ServiceWorkers on the affected host, and isolate if an executable landed. 3) Hunt: expand to the full 96-domain list, generalize the hunt to any domain where a single client fetched /sw.js then /config then received a same-origin attachment download, and correlate the originating malicious ad-referral.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — Malvertising Sends Malware in Pieces, Then Makes the Browser Build the Executabl Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Malvertising Sends Malware in Pieces, Then Makes the Browser Build the Executabl
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("app.js", "streamsaver.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("app.js", "streamsaver.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).

SourTrade browser-assembled .exe downloaded from campaign landing domains AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a browser writing an executable to disk whose mark-of-the-web origin URL is one of the confirmed SourTrade malvertising landing domains (fake TradingView/Solana/Luno). Because the malware is assembled in-memory and delivered via a same-origin ServiceWorker download, the dropped .exe carries the landing domain as its FileOriginUrl — the single cleanest host-side artifact of this technique. Rationale: Uses the 11 Confiant-confirmed SourTrade landing/staging domains as FileOriginUrl/FileOriginReferrerUrl on a browser-written .exe — the exact host-side residue of the same-origin ServiceWorker download. Splunk falls back to the 3 confirmed SHA256s since CIM Endpoint.Filesystem carries no origin-URL field. Cross-checked Confiant blog + The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html • https://gbhackers.com/sourtrade-browser-assembled/
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or threat-intel team intentionally detonating a SourTrade sample on a lab endpoint that ships MDE telemetry
  • Automated sandbox/detonation VM fetching the landing page for classification
  • A takedown/sinkhole researcher who now controls one of the listed domains serving a benign page
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platform re-hosting a lookalike lure on one of these domains
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the DeviceName/user, confirm the .exe FolderPath (Downloads/Temp), grab its SHA256 and check whether the process has already executed (DeviceProcessEvents on that hash/path). 2) Contain: isolate the host in MDE, quarantine/delete the dropped .exe, and block the source domain + its resolved IPs at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the other 10 domains (see C2 UC), for any Bun-runtime executable running under a non-bun name (see execution UC), and for credential-theft follow-on (browser cookie-store access, wallet-file reads).
DeviceFileEvents

| where FileName endswith ".exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","chromium.exe")
| where FileOriginUrl has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","lunavo.club","authcom.digital","form-engine.digital","trustconnect.digital","predictcore.digital")
   or FileOriginReferrerUrl has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","lunavo.club","authcom.digital","form-engine.digital","trustconnect.digital","predictcore.digital")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
